description: Evidence that each nation was forced to move, for every journey in removals.json: A, the order (treaty, statute or military order); B, the move itself as recorded at the time (dates, numbers, deaths); C, the force or coercion, or records showing the move was negotiated or voluntary; and links to the nation's own account (not quoted). The six pilot journeys were gathered Nov. 27, 2026 by two research subagents; the other 49 later the same day by seven regional research subagents. Every quotation was re-matched by script (scripts/removals/check_evidence_quotes.py) against the text fetched (scripts/removals/fetch_source.py); the result is in each item's "checked" field. Review status: Unverified.
findings_description: One judgment per journey, by the thread session from the evidence below (project analysis, Unverified). move: forced (troops, prisoners, escorts or orders to kill), pressured (state laws, settlers, hunger or threats, without troops), negotiated (a treaty move the record shows as agreed or chosen), or not carried out. record: how strong the contemporary record of the move and the force is. arrow: solid when the journey has an order (A) and a record of the move made at the time (B); dashed when the move itself is not yet found; not carried out for removals that never happened.
fields_description: Added Nov. 28, 2026 for the Removals page, to every item that is shown (not catalog-only or memory): date (when the record itself was made, YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM or YYYY, from the item’s own citation and description), sentence (one plain sentence on what the record shows), source (the citation of the whole document, without the pinpoint, which numbers the References), and for a nation’s account, title (its page’s name). no_account marks a nation’s link whose pages were not found to give an account of the removal; it is kept here and left off the page. Drafted by script and a model from each item’s own fields, then checked by script (each date’s year, month and day appear in the item) and spot-checked; Unverified.

cherokee-arkansas-emigration.summary: Negotiated with the Arkansas Cherokee; settler pressure and withheld improvement pay pushed dissenters to go. Not a forced move in the record.

cherokee-removal.summary: General Scott's troops rounded up about 6,000 prisoners into 23 posts and sent them west in detachments, the last leaving Dec. 4, 1838.

choctaw-arkansas-1820.summary: A voluntary emigration offer, mostly not carried out; the tract was cut back in 1825 because settlers were already on it.

choctaw-removal.summary: Mississippi extended its laws over the Choctaw and sent constables and sheriffs onto their land; removal agents recorded the parties, their numbers and their suffering. No troops recorded.

chickasaw-removal.summary: The 1832 treaty recites that the Chickasaw were oppressed by state laws; five to six hundred died of smallpox on the way (Armstrong, 1838). No troops recorded and no total moved found.

creek-mcintosh-emigration.summary: Voluntary emigration of McIntosh's followers, who "fled their country" after their break with the Creek Nation; about 2,400 went in two parties.

creek-removal.summary: After the 1836 hostilities the Secretary of War ordered the Creeks removed "whether willing or unwilling to go"; the Commissioner reported all removed but the families of 700 warriors.

seminole-removal.summary: Agent Thompson told the chiefs the President "will compel you to go"; war followed, and over 2,000 had been carried west by 1839.

seminole-florida-1858.summary: After twenty years of war, Billy Bowlegs and 163 followers were induced to go by payment in 1858; four died on the way.

apalachicola-removal.summary: Blunt's band chose to emigrate under the 1832 and 1833 treaties, at its own cost; two upper-town chiefs refused. Departure date and numbers not found.

potawatomi-chicago-1833.summary: The treaty is solid, but no record of the 1835 move itself was found; the record shows only reluctance to sell.

potawatomi-indiana-removal.summary: The Commissioner's 1838 report: the Potawatomi showed "an indisposition to comply" and General Tipton's 100 volunteers carried out the collection and removal of 768 people.

potawatomi-trail-of-death.summary: Indiana militia under General Tipton gathered about 859 Potawatomi and marched them to Kansas, Sept. 4 to Nov. 4, 1838; about 43 died.

potawatomi-kansas-1846.summary: The 1846 move from Council Bluffs was negotiated; the 1867 move was optional by register, under settler pressure.

hochunk-removal.summary: Over two regiments of infantry spent the summer of 1840 "forcing a large majority of them across the Mississippi"; in 1848 a third of the tribe fled the removal party.

sauk-fox-removal.summary: In 1831 General Gaines's troops and Illinois militia removed Black Hawk's band west of the Mississippi; the Governor said "peaceably, if they can: but forcibly, if they must."

kickapoo-removal.summary: Treaty removals of bands recited as willing to go; 375 Kickapoo moved in 1833. No force found.

shawnee-missouri-kansas.summary: Treaty only; no record of the move or of force was found.

shawnee-ohio-kansas.summary: A government-run treaty emigration of about 450 Shawnee, Sept. to Nov. 1832, without troops; their request to travel by land was refused.

seneca-sandusky-removal.summary: The removal agent wrote "I charge myself with cruelty in forcing these unfortunate people on"; measles and deaths on the road, 1831-1832. No troops.

seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.summary: The band was recorded as willing to go; the government controlled only the manner of travel. One death recorded.

lenape-removal.summary: Treaty removals over fifty years; an agent wrote in 1830 that the Delaware would not go without "some appearance of compulsion." Little record of the early moves.

wyandot-removal.summary: 664 Wyandot left Upper Sandusky July 12, 1843, and about 100 died within a year; the Commissioner called the move "purely voluntary."

miami-removal.summary: The Commissioner: "there was no alternative but to send troops to compel" the Miami; 323 left Peru, Indiana, under troops on Oct. 6, 1846.

ottawa-ohio-removal.summary: Treaty removal of about 100 Ottawa in 1832, struck by cholera; one band was left free to go when it chose.

peoria-wea-piankashaw-removal.summary: Treaty cessions and relocations; the Indiana Wea refused to go in 1832, and the 1867 move was framed as a request.

ny-kansas-removal.summary: The Seneca protested the 1838 treaty as obtained by "fraud, bribery, perjury, and forgery"; the 1846 party to Kansas was small and volunteer: of 271, 82 died and 94 returned.

ny-wisconsin-migration.summary: A chosen move: the Stockbridge themselves petitioned that they had determined to seek a new home in the west.

stockbridge-1848-attempt.summary: The tribe refused to go to Minnesota; the 1856 treaty gave them land in Wisconsin instead.

menominee-attempted-removal.summary: The removal to Crow Wing, Minnesota never happened; the 1854 treaty recites the Menominee's "great unwillingness" to go. They were moved within Wisconsin in 1852.

osage-removal.summary: The 1870 act required Osage consent; the council accepted under white encroachment, and 3,956 were on the new reserve in 1872.

kaw-removal.summary: The 1872 act required the tribe's agreement; intruders and starvation were the pressure. They left June 4 and arrived June 21, 1873, without a death.

quapaw-removal.summary: Concentration with the Caddo under the 1824 treaty failed; the 1833 treaty recites that nearly a quarter of the people died and they had "no alternative but to perish."

caddo-removal.summary: A negotiated 1835 cession with a removal clause; no government record of the move or of force was found.

texas-reserves-removal.summary: Settlers threatened extermination, and about 1,430 people of the Brazos and Comanche reserves were moved under army escort to the Washita, Aug. 1 to 16, 1859.

tonkawa-removal.summary: A relief move of landless, starving people under the Act of July 4, 1884; the move itself is not dated in the record found.

ponca-removal.summary: Troops from Fort Randall; 158 of 581 died within a year (Standing Bear v. Crook); an 1881 commission found the removal "without lawful authority."

pawnee-removal.summary: The Pawnee asked to go after Sioux raids killed 69 in 1873 and famine followed; about 1,800 were removed to the Wichita agency.

otoe-missouria-removal.summary: The 1881 act required consent in council; an agent warned those who refused. 70 wagons left Oct. 5 and reached Red Rock Oct. 23, 1881.

iowa-removal.summary: The 1836 treaty was an exchange the tribes are recited as having asked for; the 1883 order only confirmed a reserve where many already lived.

sac-fox-missouri-removal.summary: Only the 1836 treaty was found; no record of the move or of force.

hochunk-1863-removal.summary: Congress ordered the Winnebago out of Minnesota though they were found blameless; 1,945 were taken to Crow Creek, and the Commissioner wrote that the removal was "the result of the overwhelming pressure of the public sentiment."

dakota-1863-removal.summary: After internment at Fort Snelling under military guard, 1,306 Dakota were shipped to Crow Creek, arriving May 30, 1863; the Secretary of the Interior called them captives.

navajo-long-walk.summary: Carleton's orders to kill Navajo men who did not surrender; 8,354 Navajo counted at Bosque Redondo in 1864; 197 died on one march.

mescalero-bosque-redondo.summary: Carleton's 1862 order that Mescalero men be killed wherever found; 405 Mescalero held at Bosque Redondo in 1864.

chiricahua-exile.summary: In 1886 the whole Chiricahua and Warm Springs people, including those who had not fought, were seized by troops and sent as prisoners of war to Florida; later moves thinly recorded.

yavapai-exodus.summary: About 1,400 Yavapai and Tonto Apache were marched about 180 miles to San Carlos in 1875 on the President's order under cavalry escort; the agent wrote that they were opposed to going.

nez-perce-exile.summary: Joseph's people were held as prisoners of war and sent to Fort Leavenworth and the Indian Territory; more than a quarter died within months (Commissioner, 1878).

modoc-removal.summary: After the Modoc War, 152 prisoners were taken by the army to Fort McPherson and then to the Quapaw agency in Nov. 1873.

northern-cheyenne-removal.summary: 937 Northern Cheyenne went south under military escort in 1877, reluctantly by the Senate committee's finding; in 1879 the army tried to "starve and freeze these captives into submission" at Fort Robinson.

malheur-paiute-removal.summary: 543 Paiute held as prisoners of war were marched by cavalry to the Yakama reservation in the winter of 1878-1879, including a band that had not fought.

uintah-ute-removal.summary: The 1864 act provided for Utes who "may be induced" to go to Uintah; the pressure was settlers and hunger, not troops.

white-river-ute-removal.summary: Removed under the 1880 agreement after the Meeker killings; the troop record is for the Uncompahgre, turned over to General Mackenzie in 1881.

nome-cult-trail.summary: Settlers resolved that Indians left after thirty days should be killed; Captain Starr's troops marched 461 people from Chico, and 277 reached Round Valley, "thirty dying en route."

rogue-river-removal.summary: The bands surrendered as prisoners of war and were taken under troop escort to the Coast reservation in 1856; earlier stages were negotiated.

cherokee-removal.description: Indian Removal Act, sec. 1: President authorized to divide western lands into districts for tribes that "may choose to exchange" and remove.
cherokee-removal.quote: into a suitable number of districts, for the reception of such tribes or nations of Indians as may choose to exchange the lands where they now reside, and remove there;
cherokee-removal.notes: The Act is permissive on its face (tribes "as may choose to exchange"); it authorizes exchange and aid but does not itself order any nation to move. The compulsion came through treaties and enforcement. Sec. 7 proviso: "nothing in this act contained shall be construed as authorizing or directing the violation of any existing treaty".

cherokee-removal.sentence: The Indian Removal Act authorizes the President to set aside western districts for nations that choose to exchange their lands.

choctaw-removal.description: Indian Removal Act, sec. 1 (statutory authority for Choctaw and other exchanges).
choctaw-removal.quote: into a suitable number of districts, for the reception of such tribes or nations of Indians as may choose to exchange the lands where they now reside, and remove there;
choctaw-removal.notes: The Act is permissive on its face (tribes "as may choose to exchange"); it authorizes exchange and aid but does not itself order any nation to move. The compulsion came through treaties and enforcement. Sec. 7 proviso: "nothing in this act contained shall be construed as authorizing or directing the violation of any existing treaty".

chickasaw-removal.quote: the Chickasaw nation do hereby cede, to the United States, all the land which they own on the east side of the Mississippi river, including all the country where they at present live and occupy.

chickasaw-removal.description: Treaty of Doaksville, Jan. 17, 1837, art. 1: the Chickasaws may form a district within the Choctaw country (the treaty that fixed the destination).
chickasaw-removal.citation: Treaty with the Choctaw and Chickasaw, Jan. 17, 1837, art. 1, 11 Stat. 573

chickasaw-removal.description: Preamble of the 1832 treaty (signed by the nation): the Chickasaws state they are oppressed by being made subject to state laws and prefer to seek a home west.
chickasaw-removal.citation: Treaty with the Chickasaw, Oct. 20, 1832, preamble, 7 Stat. 381
chickasaw-removal.quote: Chickasaw Nation find themselves oppressed in their present situation; by being made subject to the laws of the States in which they reside.
chickasaw-removal.notes: Treaty text drafted by the U.S. commissioner (Gen. Coffee); shows the state-law pressure but is not a neutral finding.

chickasaw-removal.source: Treaty with the Chickasaw, Oct. 20, 1832, 7 Stat. 381

chickasaw-removal.description: Secretary of War Eaton to Gen. Coffee, Mar. 31, 1831: if no acceptable western home is found, the Chickasaws must stay and suffer subjection to state laws (the state-law lever the government used).
chickasaw-removal.citation: Letter, J. H. Eaton to Gen. John Coffee, Mar. 31, 1831, in Correspondence on the Subject of the Emigration of Indians, S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 2, at 274 (1835)
chickasaw-removal.quote: If a suitable and approved home cannot be provided, they must abide where they are, and suffer all the inconveniences which subjection to State laws must impose.

chickasaw-removal.sentence: Secretary of War Eaton tells General Coffee that without an approved home the Chickasaw must suffer state laws.
chickasaw-removal.source: Correspondence on the Subject of the Emigration of Indians, S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 2 (1835)

chickasaw-removal.description: The Chickasaw chiefs' own reply to the President at Franklin, Tenn., Aug. 25, 1830: the nation says it has lived on its land from time immemorial and is being asked to seek a home in the West.
chickasaw-removal.citation: Chickasaw delegates' reply, Franklin, Aug. 25, 1830, in Correspondence on the Subject of the Emigration of Indians, S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 2, at about 243 (1835)
chickasaw-removal.quote: we, the Chickasaws, have occupied the country, not only where we now live, from time immemorial

chickasaw-removal.sentence: The Chickasaw delegates reply that their nation has lived on its land from time immemorial.
chickasaw-removal.source: Correspondence on the Subject of the Emigration of Indians, S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 2 (1835)

creek-removal.citation: Treaty with the Creeks, Mar. 24, 1832, art. XII, 7 Stat. 366

seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.description: Indian Removal Act, May 28, 1830: the President may lay off districts west of the Mississippi 'for the reception of such tribes or nations of Indians as may choose to exchange' their lands. The text is permissive; the force came from how the treaties were then obtained and carried out.
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.quote: for the reception of such tribes or nations of Indians as may choose to exchange the lands where they now reside, and remove there
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.notes: Pin is the first page of the act. The statute itself does not compel any nation to move; cited as the authority the treaties recite.
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.sentence: The President may set aside districts west of the Mississippi for Native nations that choose to exchange their lands.

seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.description: Journal of the conductors of the 'Lewistown detachment' (Aug. 20 - Dec. 13, 1832): the party left Lewistown, Ohio, about Sept. 19, 1832, and was handed over at the Seneca agency on Dec. 13, 1832, after a winter march by horseback and wagon.
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.citation: Journal of D. M. Workman and D. R. Dunihue, in S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 4, at 84 (1834).
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.quote: the agent for the Senecas, agreeably to instruction. They will remain upon the land of their brethren, the Senecas, until an exchange of their tract of land is made
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.dates: left Lewistown c. Sept. 19, 1832; reached Seneca agency Dec. 13, 1832
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.notes: Page 84 by the scan's running page number. The conductors' full sentence is 'I delivered the Indians into the care of Major Kennerly, the agent for the Senecas, agreeably to instruction'; the scan misprints 'Kennerly', so the quote starts after the name.
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)

seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.citation: Journal of D. M. Workman and D. R. Dunihue, in S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 4, at 82 (1834).
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.quote: A child died this morning, (the only death which has occured in this tribe,) which detained us until late.
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.notes: Low mortality was recorded for this detachment. Compare the Sandusky Seneca (nine deaths in the last stretch alone).

seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.description: The band asked to travel by land, on horseback: the chief told Lt. Lane that 'it is useless to try to persuade them to go by steamboats', while the War Department insisted that 'the plan of removal by steamboat is unalterable' (see Gibson order). In the end the detachment went overland.
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.citation: Journal of D. M. Workman and D. R. Dunihue, Aug. 21, 1832, in S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 4, at 78 (1834).
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.quote: They are ready, willing, and anxious to go, and always have been; but it is useless to try to persuade them to go by steamboats.
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.notes: Cuts both ways: the band says it is 'ready, willing, and anxious to go' (voluntary) while the government tried to dictate the manner. Some old women said they would rather stay and die than go by steamboat or wagon (OCR of that passage is poor, so not quoted).
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.sentence: The chief tells Lieutenant Lane the band is ready to go, but persuading it to travel by steamboat is useless.
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.source: Journal of D. M. Workman and D. R. Dunihue, in S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 4 (1834)

seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.description: Gen. Gibson's order to the superintendent for all the Ohio parties: the President will not allow land travel; 'the plan of removal by steamboat is unalterable'.
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.citation: Gen. George Gibson, quoted in Gardiner to Sec'y of War Cass, in S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 4, at 112 (1834).
seneca-shawnee-lewistown-removal.quote: but, above all, say that the plan of removal by steamboat is unalterable.

lenape-removal.description: Treaty of St. Marys, Oct. 3, 1818, art. 2: the Delaware cede their Indiana land and the United States agrees to provide a country west of the Mississippi.
lenape-removal.citation: Treaty with the Delawares, Oct. 3, 1818, art. 2, 7 Stat. 188.
lenape-removal.quote: the United States agree to provide for the Delawares a country to reside in, upon the west side of the Mississippi, and to guaranty to them the peaceable possession of the same
lenape-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
lenape-removal.sentence: The Delaware cede their Indiana land and the United States agrees to provide a country west of the Mississippi.

lenape-removal.description: Treaty of Sept. 24, 1829: the Delaware are 'now willing to remove' from the James Fork of White River, Missouri, to the fork of the Kansas and Missouri rivers.
lenape-removal.citation: Treaty with the Delawares, Sept. 24, 1829, 7 Stat. 327.
lenape-removal.quote: whereas the said Delaware Nation, are now willing to remove, on the following conditions, from the country on James fork of White river in the State of Missouri, to the Country selected in the fork of the Kansas and Missouri River
lenape-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
lenape-removal.sentence: The Delaware are now willing to remove from James Fork in Missouri to the fork of the Kansas and Missouri rivers.

lenape-removal.description: Treaty of July 4, 1866, preamble: Congress had made it the President's duty 'to provide by treaty for the removal of the Indian tribes from the State of Kansas', and the Delaware had 'expressed a wish' to remove to the Indian country.
lenape-removal.citation: Treaty with the Delawares, July 4, 1866, preamble, 14 Stat. 793.
lenape-removal.quote: Whereas Congress has by law made it the duty of the President of the United States to provide by treaty for the removal of the Indian tribes from the State of Kansas; and whereas the Delaware Indians have expressed a wish to remove from their present reservation in said State to the Indian country
lenape-removal.notes: A state-policy removal in the treaty's own words. Passage is 59 words.
lenape-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
lenape-removal.sentence: The treaty recites that Congress made it the President's duty to arrange removal of Native nations from Kansas, and the Delaware wish to go.
lenape-removal.source: Treaty with the Delawares, July 4, 1866, 14 Stat. 793

lenape-removal.description: Stage 3: the Delaware agent's 1869 report: the Delaware are now in the Cherokee country on the Verdigris; 'the aged and weak have suffered for want of suitable shelter, and some have sickened and died; but the mortality has been small'; the tribe numbered 1,005.
lenape-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1869, at 375 (Gov't Printing Off. 1870).
lenape-removal.quote: As is generally the case in removing tribes, the aged and weak have suffered for want of suitable shelter, and some have sickened and died . . . the mortality has been small.
lenape-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
lenape-removal.sentence: The Delaware agent reports that the aged and weak suffered for want of shelter, and some died, but mortality was small.
lenape-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1869 (Gov't Printing Off. 1870)

lenape-removal.description: Ohio agent McElvain on the Sandusky Delaware, Sept. 20, 1830: they would not all go without 'some appearance of compulsion'. He says that course would be 'imprudent' at that time.
lenape-removal.citation: John McElvain to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, Sept. 20, 1830, in S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 2, at 110 (1834).
lenape-removal.quote: I am now convinced that it is useless to think to remove them all at the same time, without holding out to them some appearance of compulsion
lenape-removal.notes: McElvain's next words: 'but such a course at this time would be imprudent'. The same letter says the full-blooded Delaware 'are anxious to remove' while the mixed-blood chief held the rest back for annuity reasons. Page approximate.
lenape-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
lenape-removal.sentence: Agent McElvain says removing all the Sandusky Delaware at once needs some appearance of compulsion, which he calls imprudent.
lenape-removal.source: S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 2 (1834)

lenape-removal.description: The 1832 treaty with the Cape Girardeau Delaware admits that in 1815 'it became necessary for them to remove, leaving their fields and improvements' and that the United States wished 'to indemnify the said Delawares for all losses and injuries by them sustained in consequence of such removal'.
lenape-removal.citation: Treaty with the Shawnee and Delaware, Oct. 26, 1832, preamble, 7 Stat. 397.
lenape-removal.quote: it being the desire of the United States to indemnify the said Delawares for all losses and injuries by them sustained in consequence of such removal
lenape-removal.notes: Official recognition of loss caused by an earlier forced-in-effect departure from Missouri; the cause is given only as 'various causes'.
lenape-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
lenape-removal.sentence: The treaty says the United States wishes to indemnify the Delaware for losses sustained in consequence of their removal.
lenape-removal.source: Treaty with the Shawnee and Delaware, Oct. 26, 1832, 7 Stat. 397

lenape-removal.description: Delaware agent, Sept. 19, 1866: the tribe had for two years been 'expecting to remove from their present reservation', which made them 'still more indifferent to effort'; they wished to go where 'game is abundant'.
lenape-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1866, at 247 (Gov't Printing Off. 1866).
lenape-removal.quote: The Delawares for the last two years have been expecting to remove from their present reservation, and the influence has been to render those habitually indolent still more indifferent to effort.
lenape-removal.notes: The same report says 'the desire is to remove to a home more remote'. So the Delaware agent records the Delaware as willing, but only after a federal removal policy and railroad sales.
lenape-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
lenape-removal.sentence: The Delaware agent says two years of expecting removal has left the habitually indolent even more indifferent to effort.
lenape-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1866 (Gov't Printing Off. 1866)

lenape-removal.description: Kansas legislature, Feb. 1870: it pressed Congress for 'the speedy removal of all Indians who have not become citizens' from Kansas.
lenape-removal.citation: Resolutions of the Legislature of Kansas, Feb. 4, 1870, S. Misc. Doc., 41st Cong., 2d Sess. (Serial 1408, doc. 56).
lenape-removal.quote: our senators in Congress are hereby instructed and our representative requested to use their influence to obtain such legislation as will secure the speedy removal of all Indian tribes from our State
lenape-removal.notes: Dated after the Delaware had moved (1867-68) but shows the state's policy, in the same period, that the 1866 treaty recites.
lenape-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
lenape-removal.sentence: The Kansas legislature instructs its senators to seek the speedy removal of all Native nations from the state.
lenape-removal.source: Resolutions of the Legislature of Kansas, Feb. 4, 1870, S. Misc. Doc., 41st Cong., 2d Sess. (Serial 1408, doc. 56)

wyandot-removal.description: Treaty of Mar. 17, 1842: the Wyandot cede all their Ohio land (109,144 acres) and Michigan land, and the United States grants them 148,000 acres west of the Mississippi on Indian land.
wyandot-removal.citation: Treaty with the Wyandot, Mar. 17, 1842, art. 2, 11 Stat. 581.
wyandot-removal.quote: the United States hereby grant to the aforesaid Wyandott Nation a tract of land west of the Mississippi River, to contain one hundred and forty-eight thousand acres

wyandot-removal.description: Gardiner pressing the Wyandot chiefs at Upper Sandusky in May 1831: he urged them to go west, 'the chiefs were taken by surprise, and declined the offer', and he then threatened to buy out each adult man's interest in the reservation separately.
wyandot-removal.citation: John McElvain to Sec'y of War Eaton, Columbus, May 22, 1831, in S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 2, at 459 (1834).
wyandot-removal.quote: After the chiefs assembled, Mr. Gardiner with great energy urged them to remove to the west; the chiefs were taken by surprise, and declined the offer.
wyandot-removal.notes: This is an attempt that failed in 1831; the Wyandot ceded in 1842. McElvain's next paragraph: 'This declaration mortified and surprised the chiefs'. Page approximate.
wyandot-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
wyandot-removal.sentence: Special agent James Gardiner urges the Wyandot chiefs to go west, then threatens to buy out each adult man's interest.
wyandot-removal.source: S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 2 (1834)

wyandot-removal.description: The same agent warned that if the Ohio tribes were 'crowded to sell their lands', many would go to Canada instead; a statement of the pressure being applied.
wyandot-removal.citation: McElvain to Eaton, May 22, 1831, in S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 2, at 459 (1834).
wyandot-removal.quote: if this is not granted, and they are at the present time crowded to sell their lands, many of them will most assuredly remove to Canada
wyandot-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
wyandot-removal.sentence: Agent McElvain warns that if the Ohio nations are crowded to sell their lands, many will go to Canada.

wyandot-removal.description: Commissioner Crawford (Nov. 16, 1842): the 1842 treaty 'has been the object of the Department for years to effect' and is 'important to the State of Ohio'; the Indians may use their land only until Apr. 1, 1844, after which it will be sold to citizens. States the purpose of the cession and removal.
wyandot-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, Nov. 16, 1842, in H.R. Doc. No. 2, 27th Cong., 3d Sess., at 372 (1842).
wyandot-removal.quote: Department for years to effect, is justly regarded to be important to the State of Ohio, and particularly to that portion of it in which the Wyandots reside
wyandot-removal.notes: The quotation begins at the top of page 372 after a page break (the sentence starts 'The consummation of this measure, which it has been the object of the' on p. 371). The nation was not forced by troops. The deadline in art. 7 was the pressure.
wyandot-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
wyandot-removal.sentence: Commissioner Crawford calls the Wyandot cession important to Ohio and says the land will be sold to citizens after the deadline.
wyandot-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, Nov. 16, 1842, in H.R. Doc. No. 2, 27th Cong., 3d Sess. (1842)

wyandot-removal.description: The Commissioner's own finding cuts the other way: the Wyandot movement 'was conducted by themselves exclusively . . . and was of course purely voluntary'. This is the government's contemporary description and must be weighed against the 1831 pressure and the treaty cession of all Ohio land.
wyandot-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, Nov. 25, 1843, in S. Doc. No. 1, 28th Cong., 1st Sess., at 262 (1843).
wyandot-removal.quote: The movement was conducted by themselves exclusively . . . and was of course purely voluntary.
wyandot-removal.notes: Honest counter-evidence. The full sentence is: 'The movement was conducted by themselves exclusively—was in anticipation of the time (1st of April, 1844) at which their treaty obligations bound them to emigrate, and was of course purely voluntary.'
wyandot-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
wyandot-removal.sentence: The Commissioner says the Wyandot conducted their own move, which was purely voluntary.
wyandot-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, Nov. 25, 1843, in S. Doc. No. 1, 28th Cong., 1st Sess. (1843)

wyandot-removal.description: The Wyandot chiefs' own memorial to Congress (Jan. 20, 1846) says they 'have been greatly aggrieved by the course pursued towards them by the United States, in regard to their late treaty for the cession of all their lands in Ohio and Michigan'. The grievance is unpaid improvements, not the move itself.
wyandot-removal.citation: Memorial of the Chiefs and Delegates of the Wyandot Indians, S. Doc. No. 136, 29th Cong., 1st Sess., at 1 (Jan. 20, 1846).
wyandot-removal.quote: That the Wyandot Indians .have been greatly aggrieved by the course pursued towards them by the United States, in regard to their late treaty for the cession of all their lands in Ohio and Michigan.
wyandot-removal.notes: The scan has a stray period before 'have' which is copied as printed in the OCR. A Senate committee report (S. Rep. No. 135, same session) agreed the government owed them the full value of improvements; it also records that receipts were 'extorted from them by reason of their poverty'.
wyandot-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
wyandot-removal.sentence: The Wyandot chiefs tell Congress they were greatly aggrieved by the government's treatment under their Ohio and Michigan treaty.
wyandot-removal.source: Memorial of the Chiefs and Delegates of the Wyandot Indians, S. Doc. No. 136, 29th Cong., 1st Sess. (Jan. 20, 1846)

miami-removal.description: Sub-agent Joseph Sinclear, Oct. 14, 1846, aboard the steamer Colorado near Evansville: a detachment of U.S. troops under Capt. Jouett arrived at Peru, Indiana, Sept. 26, and the Miami left Peru on Oct. 6.

miami-removal.quote: A detachment of United States troops, under the command of Captain Jouett, arrived at Peru on the 26th September, and the Miamies left that point on the 6th of October.

miami-removal.notes: The same report (pp. 3-4) says the removal 'could not be effected without incurring the expense of sending a company of troops to coerce them into a compliance with their treaty stipulations' and that 'the mere presence of the troops was sufficient'. ny-kansas-removal.description: Same report: the committee notes that the tribe was divided into emigrating and non-emigrating parties and the agent had trouble before the required number could be enrolled; also smallpox cost.
ny-kansas-removal.quote: The tribe being divided into emigrating and non-emigrating parties, the agent had much trouble, and was subjected to much annoyance, before the required number could be enrolled for removal
ny-kansas-removal.notes: Shows the 1846 party was recruited from volunteers with difficulty; this supports the plain finding that the Kansas move itself was not a forced march.

ny-kansas-removal.description: Court of Claims findings, adopted in the Supreme Court's opinion, from Hogeboom's muster roll in the Indian Office: 271 mustered, 191 arrived in Kansas June 15, 1846, 82 died and 94 returned to New York.
ny-kansas-removal.citation: New York Indians v. United States, 170 U.S. 1, 12 (1898) (quoting finding of the Court of Claims)
ny-kansas-removal.quote: From Hogeboom’s muster-roll, in the Indian Office, it appears that 271 were mustered for emigration. The roll shows that of this number 73 did not leave New York with the party; 191 only arrived in Kansas, June 15, 1846; 17 other Indians arrived subsequently; 82 died and 94 returned to New York
ny-kansas-removal.numbers: 271 mustered; 191 arrived in Kansas June 15, 1846; 17 more arrived later
ny-kansas-removal.deaths: 82 died (of the 271 mustered), per the muster roll as summarised
ny-kansas-removal.notes: Later judicial summary of the Indian Office muster roll, not the roll itself. The roll is in the National Archives (not fetched). Pin page approximate (the findings are printed at the start of the report, roughly pp. 3-12). The CAP text has OCR noise, but the quoted passage is clean.

ny-kansas-removal.sentence: The Supreme Court quotes a finding that 191 of 271 mustered New York Indians reached Kansas.
ny-kansas-removal.source: New York Indians v. United States, 170 U.S. 1 (1898)

ny-kansas-removal.description: The Seneca chiefs' own protest to the Senate, Dec. 1839: the 1838 treaty was obtained by fraud, bribery, perjury and forgery. This is the nation's own contemporaneous protest.
ny-kansas-removal.citation: Memorial of a Number of the Chief Warriors and Chiefs of the Six and Seneca Nations of Indians, S. Doc. No. 33, 26th Cong., 1st Sess. 1 (1839) (Serial 355)
ny-kansas-removal.quote: that fraud, bribery, perjury, and forgery, have been practised in order to obtain the treaty
ny-kansas-removal.notes: Signed by about 80 chiefs, certified Dec. 16, 1839 at the Buffalo Creek reservation.
ny-kansas-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
ny-kansas-removal.sentence: The Seneca chiefs tell the Senate that fraud, bribery, perjury and forgery have been practiced to obtain the Buffalo Creek treaty.
ny-kansas-removal.source: Memorial of a Number of the Chief Warriors and Chiefs of the Six and Seneca Nations of Indians, S. Doc. No. 33, 26th Cong., 1st Sess. (1839) (Serial 355)

ny-kansas-removal.description: President Van Buren's message to the Senate (Jan. 13, 1840), quoted in the Quakers' memorial to the House: improper means were used to obtain the assent of the Seneca chiefs. The President is an official finding that the assent was not fairly obtained.
ny-kansas-removal.citation: Memorial of Benjamin Ferris on behalf of the four yearly meetings of Friends, H.R. Doc. No. 66, 26th Cong., 2d Sess. 2 (1841) (quoting Message of Jan. 13, 1840) (Serial 383)
ny-kansas-removal.quote: That improper means have been employed to obtain the assent of the Seneca chiefs, there is every reason to believe
ny-kansas-removal.notes: The message itself (Jan. 13, 1840) was not fetched; the words are quoted from it by the Friends. Written by non-Native petitioners, so a secondary witness to the President's words. The Senate committee also reported against ratification (same page).
ny-kansas-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
ny-kansas-removal.sentence: President Van Buren tells the Senate that improper means have been used to obtain the Seneca chiefs' assent.
ny-kansas-removal.source: Memorial of Benjamin Ferris on behalf of the four yearly meetings of Friends, H.R. Doc. No. 66, 26th Cong., 2d Sess. (1841) (Serial 383)

ny-kansas-removal.description: Tonawanda Seneca petition to the President and Senate (1846): they unanimously opposed both treaties and resisted their execution; they ask that the treaties be abrogated. Transmitted by President Polk.
ny-kansas-removal.citation: Message from the President Communicating a Petition of the Tonawanda Band of Seneca Indians, S. Doc. No. 273, 29th Cong., 1st Sess. 2 (1846) (Serial 474)
ny-kansas-removal.quote: That we did unanimously oppose the treaty of January 15, 1S3S, and prevented its adoption in open council
ny-kansas-removal.notes: Tonawanda later made its own treaty in 1857 and kept its land. The OCR reads 'January 15, 1S3S' for 1838; quote kept exactly as the OCR shows it.
ny-kansas-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
ny-kansas-removal.sentence: The Tonawanda Seneca tell the President and Senate that they unanimously opposed and blocked the Buffalo Creek treaty.
ny-kansas-removal.source: Message from the President Communicating a Petition of the Tonawanda Band of Seneca Indians, S. Doc. No. 273, 29th Cong., 1st Sess. (1846) (Serial 474)

ny-kansas-removal.description: Court of Claims finding: the Senecas, Cayugas, Onondagas and Tuscaroras kept protesting; the Senecas said they would never emigrate but on compulsion. The finding also records that in 1846 only seven persons enrolled to emigrate at Cattaraugus.
ny-kansas-removal.citation: New York Indians v. United States, 170 U.S. 1 (1898) (findings 11-13)
ny-kansas-removal.quote: that their declaration of assent was invalid, and that they would never emigrate but on Compulsion
ny-kansas-removal.notes: A court finding that the nations refused to go, which cuts both ways for this journey: the Kansas move was small and voluntary because the nations refused, not because force was used. Capital 'C' in 'Compulsion' is as in the CAP text.
ny-kansas-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
ny-kansas-removal.sentence: The Court of Claims finds that the Seneca, Cayuga, Onondaga and Tuscarora nations protest and would emigrate only under compulsion.
ny-kansas-removal.source: New York Indians v. United States, 170 U.S. 1 (1898)

ny-wisconsin-migration.description: Menominee treaty of Feb. 8, 1831, art. 1: a tract on Lake Winnebago and Fox River is set apart as a home for the New York Indians 'who may remove to, and settle upon the same, within three years'. A permissive offer, not an order.
ny-wisconsin-migration.citation: Treaty with the Menominee, Feb. 8, 1831, art. 1, 7 Stat. 342
ny-wisconsin-migration.quote: may be set apart as a home to the several tribes of the New York Indians, who may remove to, and settle upon the same, within three years from the date of this agreement
ny-wisconsin-migration.notes: Quote shows the clause is permissive ('who may remove').
ny-wisconsin-migration.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
ny-wisconsin-migration.sentence: The Menominee treaty offers land on Lake Winnebago to New York Indians who may choose to settle there.
ny-wisconsin-migration.source: Treaty with the Menominee, Feb. 8, 1831, 7 Stat. 342

ny-wisconsin-migration.description: The Stockbridge nation's own petition to Congress (1840) says that they themselves determined to seek a new home in the west because their New York tract was too limited in extent for their wants; a party of 50 or 60 emigrated in 1818 and the nation later moved to Green Bay.
ny-wisconsin-migration.citation: Petition of the Stockbridge Nation of Indians in Wiskonsin, H.R. Doc. No. 127, 26th Cong., 1st Sess. 1-2 (1840) (Serial 365)
ny-wisconsin-migration.quote: determined to seek in the west a new home and a resting-place
ny-wisconsin-migration.dates: Party of 50-60 left 1818; main removal to Green Bay 1820s-1830s
ny-wisconsin-migration.notes: This is the nation's account made at the time. It describes a chosen move, with a land sale to New York State to finance it. It does not describe troops or compulsion. Pin pages approximate (petition begins at 1).
ny-wisconsin-migration.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
ny-wisconsin-migration.sentence: The Stockbridge nation says its New York land is too small, so it seeks a new home in the west.
ny-wisconsin-migration.source: Petition of the Stockbridge Nation of Indians in Wiskonsin, H.R. Doc. No. 127, 26th Cong., 1st Sess. (1840) (Serial 365)

ny-wisconsin-migration.description: Stage 2 context: the 1839 Stockbridge and Munsee treaty and the later emigration west. The Secretary of War reports 169 Stockbridge and Munsee who 'have lately emigrated' to the Indian territory without waiting for ratification, and asks for funds.
ny-wisconsin-migration.citation: Letter from the Secretary of War, S. Doc. No. 42, 26th Cong., 1st Sess. 1 (1840) (Serial 355)
ny-wisconsin-migration.quote: the expense of the removal and subsistence of 169 Stockbridge and. Munsee Indians, who have lately emigrated, to the Indian territory west of the Mississippi
ny-wisconsin-migration.notes: This is the 1839 emigration of part of the tribe from Wisconsin westward (not the New York-to-Wisconsin move itself). The letter quotes the 1839 treaty term that removal is paid for those 'desirous of emigrating', so that emigration was voluntary in form; the party had left before ratification.
ny-wisconsin-migration.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
ny-wisconsin-migration.sentence: The Secretary of War asks for funds to pay for the removal of 169 Stockbridge and Munsee who have emigrated.
ny-wisconsin-migration.source: Letter from the Secretary of War, S. Doc. No. 42, 26th Cong., 1st Sess. (1840) (Serial 355)

ny-wisconsin-migration.description: Stockbridge-Munsee Community's own tribal history timeline: describes the loss of lands in New York and the move to Wisconsin. (Link only.)
ny-wisconsin-migration.notes: Link only; not quoted. The timeline lists 'Series of sales to New York State dispossess Mohicans' and later removals west.
ny-wisconsin-migration.sentence: Stockbridge-Munsee Community. Its timeline covers the loss of New York lands and the move to Wisconsin.
ny-wisconsin-migration.title: Tribal History Timeline

stockbridge-1848-attempt.description: Art. 7 of the 1848 treaty: the tribe may stay one year after ratification and 'will remove to the country set apart for them, or such other west of the Mississipi River'. Art. 8 says the U.S. will pay removal costs 'whenever the said Stockbridge tribe shall signify their wish to emigrate'.
stockbridge-1848-attempt.citation: Treaty with the Stockbridge Tribe, Nov. 24, 1848, art. 7, 9 Stat. 955 (ratified Mar. 1, 1849)
stockbridge-1848-attempt.quote: that they will remove to the country set apart for them, or such other west of the Mississipi River as they may be able to secure
stockbridge-1848-attempt.notes: The clause is an undertaking to remove, but art. 8 makes the actual emigration depend on the tribe's own wish to emigrate. No date is fixed for the move and no authority to compel is given.
stockbridge-1848-attempt.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
stockbridge-1848-attempt.sentence: The Stockbridge nation agrees to remove west of the Mississippi after a stay of one year.
stockbridge-1848-attempt.source: Treaty with the Stockbridge Tribe, Nov. 24, 1848, 9 Stat. 955

stockbridge-1848-attempt.description: Art. 8: payment of removal expenses is conditional on the tribe signifying its wish to emigrate.
stockbridge-1848-attempt.citation: Treaty with the Stockbridge Tribe, Nov. 24, 1848, art. 8, 9 Stat. 955
stockbridge-1848-attempt.quote: Whenever the said Stockbridge tribe shall signify their wish to emigrate, the United States will defray the expenses of their removal west of the Mississippi
stockbridge-1848-attempt.notes: Shows removal was voluntary in form.
stockbridge-1848-attempt.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
stockbridge-1848-attempt.sentence: The United States pays removal costs only once the Stockbridge say they wish to emigrate.
stockbridge-1848-attempt.source: Treaty with the Stockbridge Tribe, Nov. 24, 1848, 9 Stat. 955

stockbridge-1848-attempt.description: The 1856 treaty's recitals record what happened: the 1848 treaty obligated the tribe to remove west, but many refused when offered a location in Minnesota and asked for the return of Stockbridge township. The removal never took place; the 1856 treaty gave a reservation in Wisconsin (Shawano County).
stockbridge-1848-attempt.citation: Treaty with the Stockbridge and Munsee, Feb. 5, 1856, preamble, 11 Stat. 663
stockbridge-1848-attempt.quote: many of the tribe refused to remove, when they were offered a location in Minnesota
stockbridge-1848-attempt.notes: The treaty is the government's own record that the 1848 removal was not carried out. The stage in removals.json (1848-1856) should be read as 'attempted, not carried out'. Note that part of the Stockbridge-Munsee had already gone west under the 1839 treaty (see ny-wisconsin-migration).
stockbridge-1848-attempt.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
stockbridge-1848-attempt.sentence: This treaty records that many Stockbridge refused to remove when offered a location in Minnesota.
stockbridge-1848-attempt.source: Treaty with the Stockbridge and Munsee, Feb. 5, 1856, 11 Stat. 663

stockbridge-1848-attempt.description: Same treaty: the majority of the tribe 'are averse to removing to Minnesota and prefer a new location in Wisconsin'.
stockbridge-1848-attempt.citation: Treaty with the Stockbridge and Munsee, Feb. 5, 1856, preamble, 11 Stat. 663
stockbridge-1848-attempt.quote: a majority of the said tribe of Stockbridges and the Munsees are averse to removing to Minnesota and prefer a new location in Wisconsin
stockbridge-1848-attempt.notes: The destination the government offered in the 1850s was Minnesota (not an unspecified land west of the Mississippi).
stockbridge-1848-attempt.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
stockbridge-1848-attempt.sentence: A majority of the Stockbridge and Munsee are averse to removing to Minnesota and prefer a new location in Wisconsin.
stockbridge-1848-attempt.source: Treaty with the Stockbridge and Munsee, Feb. 5, 1856, 11 Stat. 663

stockbridge-1848-attempt.description: The U.S. commissioner's letter transmitting the 1856 treaty (printed with it in the Kappler page, with Commissioner Manypenny's cover letter of Mar. 3, 1856) refers to $20,000 'to be paid under the amendment to the treaty of 1848 for procuring the adoption of the said amendment'. An official reference to money tied to getting the 1848 amendment adopted.
stockbridge-1848-attempt.citation: Letter transmitting treaty, in Treaty with the Stockbridge and Munsee, Feb. 5, 1856, 11 Stat. 663 (Kappler transcription, Office of Indian Affairs letters printed with the treaty)
stockbridge-1848-attempt.quote: the twenty thousand dollars to be paid under the amendment to the treaty of 1848 for procuring the adoption of the said amendment
stockbridge-1848-attempt.notes: The sentence concerns a claim by a man named Chandler on his share of that money. It points to payments to individuals, not force. Not strong; kept because it is the only official statement found on how the 1848 amendment came to be adopted. The author of the letter is not identified in the cached text.
stockbridge-1848-attempt.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
stockbridge-1848-attempt.sentence: Commissioner Manypenny's letter ties $20,000 to procuring the adoption of the amendment to the Stockbridge treaty.
stockbridge-1848-attempt.source: Treaty with the Stockbridge and Munsee, Feb. 5, 1856, 11 Stat. 663

menominee-attempted-removal.description: Treaty of Oct. 18, 1848, art. 3: in return for their Wisconsin land the Menominee are to receive $20,000 "in consideration of their removing themselves, which they agree to do," to the country on the upper Mississippi.
menominee-attempted-removal.citation: Treaty with the Menominee, Oct. 18, 1848, art. 3, 9 Stat. 952, 953
menominee-attempted-removal.quote: in consideration of their removing themselves, which they agree to do, without further cost or expense to the United States, twenty thousand dollars
menominee-attempted-removal.notes: The treaty was signed at Lake Poygan. The assigned land was in Minnesota Territory (Chippewa cession of 1847 on the Crow Wing). Pin page approx.
menominee-attempted-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
menominee-attempted-removal.sentence: The Menominee agree to remove themselves to the upper Mississippi for twenty thousand dollars.
menominee-attempted-removal.source: Treaty with the Menominee, Oct. 18, 1848, 9 Stat. 952

menominee-attempted-removal.description: Treaty of May 12, 1854 recites the 1848 clause and that on "great unwillingness" of the Menominee to remove to Crow Wing the President consented to their locating on the Wolf and Oconto Rivers instead.
menominee-attempted-removal.citation: Treaty with the Menominee, May 12, 1854, preamble, 10 Stat. 1064
menominee-attempted-removal.quote: upon manifestation of great unwillingness on the part of said Indians to remove to the country west of the Mississippi River, upon Crow Wing, which had been assigned them, and a desire to remain in the State of Wisconsin, the President consented to their locating temporarily upon the Wolf and Oconto Rivers.
menominee-attempted-removal.notes: Official finding that the move to Minnesota was dropped because the nation refused. No removal to Minnesota took place.
menominee-attempted-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
menominee-attempted-removal.sentence: The President lets the Menominee settle on the Wolf and Oconto Rivers after they show great unwillingness to remove.
menominee-attempted-removal.source: Treaty with the Menominee, May 12, 1854, 10 Stat. 1064

menominee-attempted-removal.description: Commissioner L. Lea, Nov. 27, 1850: the Menominee were expected to remove to the new Minnesota country "this year," but the season was too late after an exploring party; the President let them stay in Wisconsin until June 1, 1851.
menominee-attempted-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for 1850, H.R. Ex. Doc. No. 1, 31st Cong., 2d Sess., pt. 3, at 38 (1850)
menominee-attempted-removal.quote: It was expected that the Menomonies, for whom a location has been provided between the Winnebagoes and Chippewas, would be removed this year
menominee-attempted-removal.notes: Page read from OCR header (printed "88" = 38). Shows removal was ordered and then postponed, not carried out.
menominee-attempted-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
menominee-attempted-removal.sentence: Commissioner Lea expects the Menominee to move to Minnesota this year, but the season is too late.
menominee-attempted-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for 1850, H.R. Ex. Doc. No. 1, 31st Cong., 2d Sess., pt. 3 (1850)

menominee-attempted-removal.description: Superintendent Francis Huebschmann, Sept. 26, 1853: the 1848 treaty "contemplated" removal west of the Mississippi, but on representations to the department the Menominee were concentrated on the Upper Wolf and Oconto Rivers in Wisconsin and "removed there in November of last year" (1852).
menominee-attempted-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for 1853, S. Exec. Doc. No. 1, 33d Cong., 1st Sess., at 290 (1853) (Report of Supt. Francis Huebschmann, Sept. 26, 1853)
menominee-attempted-removal.quote: By the treaty with the Menominees, made in 1848, their removal west of the Mississippi was contemplated, but from representations made to the department it was thought preferable to concentrate them on the Upper Wolf and Oconto rivers, in this State
menominee-attempted-removal.notes: Plain finding: the removal to Minnesota was NOT carried out; the Menominee were moved within Wisconsin. Page 290 from running heads.
menominee-attempted-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
menominee-attempted-removal.sentence: Superintendent Huebschmann reports that the Menominee are concentrated on the Wolf and Oconto Rivers in Wisconsin.
menominee-attempted-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for 1853, S. Exec. Doc. No. 1, 33d Cong., 1st Sess. (1853)

menominee-attempted-removal.description: Green Bay sub-agent report, Sept. 1853, quotes head chief Oshkosh on the hardship of the 1852 relocation to Wolf River: "we have never been so poor and destitute of provisions as we are this year, after the solemn promise of the agents of the government made to us to effect our removal."
menominee-attempted-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for 1853, S. Exec. Doc. No. 1, 33d Cong., 1st Sess., at 292 (1853) (Report of the Green Bay Sub-agent, Sept. 1853)
menominee-attempted-removal.quote: after the solemn promise of the agents of the government made to us to effect our removal.
menominee-attempted-removal.notes: Oshkosh's own words as recorded by the sub-agent (name not captured). Concerns the move within Wisconsin, not to Minnesota. Page 292 from running head.
menominee-attempted-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
menominee-attempted-removal.sentence: Head chief Oshkosh says the Menominee are destitute after the government's solemn promise to effect their removal.
menominee-attempted-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for 1853, S. Exec. Doc. No. 1, 33d Cong., 1st Sess. (1853)

menominee-attempted-removal.description: Governor of Wisconsin Territory, Oct. 3, 1845, quoted by a House committee in 1846: the Wisconsin governor, in his Oct. 3, 1845 report, "recommends the removal of the Menomonies to the west of the Mississippi river." Shows the policy aim that led to the 1848 treaty.
menominee-attempted-removal.citation: H.R. Rep. No. 90, 29th Cong., 1st Sess., at 1 (1846)
menominee-attempted-removal.quote: recommends the removal of the Menomonies to the west of the Mississippi river
menominee-attempted-removal.notes: Statement of purpose by an official; the Menominee were not consulted in this report.
menominee-attempted-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
menominee-attempted-removal.sentence: The Wisconsin governor recommends removing the Menominee to the west of the Mississippi River.

menominee-attempted-removal.description: Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin, "Historical Documents" page listing the tribe's treaties of 1836, 1848, 1854 and 1856.

menominee-attempted-removal.notes: The nation's own page lists the 1848 and 1854 treaties; the interactive history page (InteractiveHistory.aspx) is script-rendered and could not be read.

osage-removal.description: Treaty of June 2, 1825: the Osage cede their Missouri and Arkansas lands and a Kansas tract is reserved to them "so long as they may choose to occupy the same". A negotiated cession with a reserve, not an order to move.
osage-removal.citation: Treaty with the Osage, June 2, 1825, art. 2, 7 Stat. 240; 2 Kappler 217 (1904).
osage-removal.quote: there shall be reserved, to, and for, the Great and Little Osage Tribes or Nations, aforesaid, so long as they may choose to occupy the same, the following described tract of land
osage-removal.notes: Operative wording is a reservation, not a removal order. Kappler page from URL slug (0217) is the treaty date, not a page; verify.
osage-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
osage-removal.sentence: The Osage cede their Missouri and Arkansas lands, reserving a Kansas tract for as long as they choose to occupy it.
osage-removal.source: Treaty with the Osage, June 2, 1825, 7 Stat. 240

osage-removal.description: Osage treaty of Sept. 29, 1865, art. 16: if the Osage agree to remove from Kansas to the Indian Territory, the diminished reserve is to be sold. This is the contingent clause the Act of July 15, 1870 (sec. 12) then made a presidential duty.
osage-removal.citation: Treaty with the Osage, Sept. 29, 1865, art. 16, 14 Stat. 687; 2 Kappler 878 (1904).
osage-removal.quote: if said Indians should agree to remove from the State of Kansas, and settle on lands to be provided for them by the United States in the Indian Territory
osage-removal.notes: Kappler page inferred from the URL slug (0878). Art. 12 of the same treaty (six months to leave the ceded trust lands and settle on the diminished reserve) is a separate, shorter move within Kansas.
osage-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
osage-removal.sentence: If the Osage agree to remove from Kansas, their diminished reserve is to be sold.
osage-removal.source: Treaty with the Osage, Sept. 29, 1865, 14 Stat. 687

osage-removal.description: Commissioner of Indian Affairs, 1870: describes the Act of July 15, 1870 as an act "requiring the President to obtain their consent" before the Osage vacate their Kansas lands and remove to the Indian Territory.
osage-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1870, at 6 (Gov't Printing Off. 1870) (describing Act of July 15, 1870, sec. 12, 16 Stat. 362).
osage-removal.quote: The presentation to the Osages of the act of Congress requiring the President to obtain their consent to vacate the lands they own in Kansas, and remove to the Indian Territory
osage-removal.notes: Page approximate (about 6; verify). The text of 16 Stat. 362 itself is only available here from the Library of Congress volume, whose text layer is doubled and cannot be quoted reliably; the act's own wording (per removals.json) is "whenever the Great and Little Osage Indians shall agree thereto, in such manner as the President shall prescribe, it shall be the duty of the President to remove said Indians from the State of Kansas". Either way the statute made the move conditional on Osage consent.
osage-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
osage-removal.sentence: The Commissioner says a statute requires the President to obtain Osage consent before they leave Kansas.
osage-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1870 (Gov't Printing Off. 1870)

osage-removal.description: Sept. 10, 1870: in national council the Osage chiefs and councilors (23 signers) accept the statute, asking to buy a larger tract from the Cherokee. The Secretary of the Interior then reports that "The Indians having consented to remove" the section binds both sides.
osage-removal.citation: Osage Indians in Kansas, H.R. Ex. Doc. No. 131, 41st Cong., 3d Sess., at 2-3 (1871) (petition of the Osage chiefs and councilors, Sept. 10, 1870).
osage-removal.quote: We accept the bill as binding upon us and our people, at the same time pray¬ ing that we may be allowed to purchase a larger tract of country from the Cherokees than that provided in the bill referred to.
osage-removal.notes: Shows consent given in council under the statute, with the chiefs' own conditions. Consent was given with the settler pressure in Kansas as the background (see C item), so "consent" should not be read as free choice.
osage-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
osage-removal.sentence: The Osage chiefs accept the statute as binding on their people and ask to buy a larger Cherokee tract.
osage-removal.source: Osage Indians in Kansas, H.R. Ex. Doc. No. 131, 41st Cong., 3d Sess. (1871)

osage-removal.description: Osage agent J. T. Gibson, Aug. 1872: the Osage settle on the new reservation between the 96th meridian and the Arkansas River; population reported as 3,956 in eight bands; most still go to the plains for the hunt; they doubt the new home is permanent.
osage-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1872, at 246 (Gov't Printing Off. 1872) (Report of J. T. Gibson, Osage Agency).
osage-removal.quote: Feeling disappointed and unsettled, but few of them were disposed to believe that their new home would be a permanent one
osage-removal.numbers: 3,956 Osage by the agent's table (ARCIA 1872 at 246)
osage-removal.notes: Gibson (the agent) writes of the move as accomplished; no deaths on the way are recorded in this report. The agent's table of bands is at 246 (total "3, 956" in OCR).
osage-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
osage-removal.sentence: Agent Gibson reports that the Osage settle on a new reservation, though few believe it will be permanent.
osage-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1872 (Gov't Printing Off. 1872)

osage-removal.description: Commissioner of Indian Affairs, 1870: the Osage "have been in great trouble in regard to the encroachments of the whites upon their lands", the background to the 1870 act and to the Osage consent.
osage-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1870, at 6 (Gov't Printing Off. 1870).
osage-removal.quote: the Osages have been in great trouble in regard to the encroachments of the whites upon their lands
osage-removal.notes: Page approximate. Settler pressure on the Kansas lands is the main "force" in the record; no troops moved the Osage.
osage-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)

osage-removal.description: Agent Gibson, 1872: the Osage went on their fall hunt "much displeased and discouraged", alleging that "another gross outrage had been perpetrated upon them by the Government" when the 96th meridian resurvey put their improvements inside the Cherokee reserve; they "submitted to another removal".
osage-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1872, at 245-46 (Gov't Printing Off. 1872) (Report of J. T. Gibson, Osage Agency).
osage-removal.quote: The Osages went immediately to the plains on their fall hunt, much displeased and discouraged
osage-removal.notes: Only the first clause is quoted to keep the match clean; the agent goes on (page break 245/246) to say the Osage "nobly relinquished their choice of laud and improvements and submitted to another removal". This is the nation's dissatisfaction as reported by a Quaker agent, not a petition.
osage-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
osage-removal.sentence: Agent Gibson reports that the Osage go on their fall hunt much displeased and submit to another removal.
osage-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1872 (Gov't Printing Off. 1872)

kaw-removal.description: Act of May 8, 1872 (17 Stat. 85, ch. 141): by its title an act "to provide for the Removal of the Kansas Tribe of Indians to the Indian Territory". Sec. 4 makes the sale of the diminished reserve and the removal depend on the tribe signifying its desire to the President.
kaw-removal.quote: An Act to provide for the Removal of the Kansas Tribe of Indians to the Indian Territory, and to dispose of their Lands in Kansas to actual Settlers.
kaw-removal.notes: Sec. 4 (17 Stat. at 86) reads, with the margin notes of the printed page interleaved in the OCR, "if said Kansas tribe of Indians shall signify to the President of the United States their desire to sell their diminished reserve . . . and to remove from the State of Kansas, and shall so agree in such manner as the President may prescribe"; it is not quoted because the margin notes break the text. The act was conditional on the tribe's agreement, and the proceeds were to provide "new homes in the Indian Territory".
kaw-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
kaw-removal.sentence: The act provides for the Kansas Tribe to remove to the Indian Territory once it signifies its desire to go.

kaw-removal.description: Commissioner of Indian Affairs, 1873: restates the act of May 8, 1872 as providing "for the removal of the Kansas tribes".
kaw-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1873, at 21-22 (Gov't Printing Off. 1873).
kaw-removal.quote: An act of Congress approved May 8, 1872, provides for the removal of the Kansas tribes
kaw-removal.notes: Page break 21/22 falls later in the same sentence; the quoted words are before it.
kaw-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
kaw-removal.sentence: The Commissioner restates that the law provides for removing the Kansas nations to the Indian Territory.
kaw-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1873 (Gov't Printing Off. 1873)

kaw-removal.description: Kaw agent Mahlon Stubbs, Sept. 1, 1873: the tribe left the old Council Grove reservation on June 4, 1873 and arrived at the new reservation on June 21 "without the loss of one member"; "a few deaths" occurred after arrival.
kaw-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1873, at 202 (Gov't Printing Off. 1873) (Report of M. Stubbs, Kaw Agency).
kaw-removal.quote: The tribe left their old reservation in Kan- sas on the 4th of Sixthmouth, and arrived here on the 21st without the loss of one mem- ber
kaw-removal.numbers: 627 Kaw (Commissioner's report, ARCIA 1872 at 89: "These Indians number 627")
kaw-removal.deaths: none on the march; "a few deaths" in the months after arrival (same report)
kaw-removal.notes: Quotation contains the OCR line-break hyphens "Kan- sas" and "mem- ber" exactly as in the text file. The agent does not give a head count of the march; the 627 figure is the Commissioner's count of the tribe in 1872.
kaw-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
kaw-removal.sentence: Agent Stubbs reports that the Kaw reach their new reservation without losing one member on the way.
kaw-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1873 (Gov't Printing Off. 1873)

kaw-removal.description: Central Superintendent Enoch Hoag, 1873: the tribe's progress was held back by "the constant expectation of being removed to the Indian Territory for three years past"; they reached the new home around midsummer.
kaw-removal.citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1873, at 200 (Gov't Printing Off. 1873) (Report of E. Hoag, Central Superintendency).
kaw-removal.quote: The improvement of this tribe has been greatly retarded by the constant expectation of being removed to the Indian Territory for three years past.
kaw-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
kaw-removal.sentence: Superintendent Hoag says the Kaw's progress is held back by the constant expectation of removal.
kaw-removal.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs for the Year 1873 (Gov't Printing Off. 1873)

kaw-removal.description: Secretary of the Interior J. D. Cox, June 20, 1870: asks Congress for $50,000 to remove the Kaw, because of "the dangers to which they have been, and are now, exposed, from intruders upon their lands".
kaw-removal.citation: Appropriation for Removal of Kaw Indians, H.R. Ex. Doc. No. 303, 41st Cong., 2d Sess., at 1 (1870).
kaw-removal.quote: but, in consequence of the dangers to which they have been, and are now, exposed, from intruders upon their lands
kaw-removal.notes: The same letter says "no arrangements have yet been made to remove the Kaws".
kaw-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
kaw-removal.sentence: Secretary Cox asks Congress for $50,000 to remove the Kaw, who are endangered by intruders on their lands.
kaw-removal.source: Appropriation for Removal of Kaw Indians, H.R. Ex. Doc. No. 303, 41st Cong., 2d Sess. (1870)

kaw-removal.description: Secretary of the Interior, Jan. 15, 1872: the Kaw are in such condition that, without special provision, "they will be exposed to suffering and starvation"; the Commissioner asks $50,000 to remove them to the Indian Territory. Agent Stubbs (Dec. 15, 1871) reports their horses dying on a failed winter hunt.
kaw-removal.citation: Kaw Indians, H.R. Ex. Doc. No. 67, 42d Cong., 2d Sess., at 1-3 (1872).
kaw-removal.quote: unless special provision be made to subsist them through the winter, they will be exposed to suffering and starvation.
kaw-removal.notes: Hardship and settler pressure, not troops. Nothing found shows the Kaw resisted or were compelled; the 1872 act made removal depend on the tribe's agreement, and Stubbs reports they were "well satisfied" with the change (ARCIA 1873 at 202).
kaw-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
kaw-removal.sentence: The Secretary of the Interior warns that the Kaw will face suffering and starvation without special provision.
kaw-removal.source: Kaw Indians, H.R. Ex. Doc. No. 67, 42d Cong., 2d Sess. (1872)

quapaw-removal.description: Treaty of Nov. 15, 1824, art. 4: the Quapaw "will hereafter be concentrated and confined to the district of country inhabited by the Caddo Indians" and must begin removing before Jan. 20, 1826; art. 5 provides rations and up to $1,000 for transport.
quapaw-removal.citation: Treaty with the Quapaw, Nov. 15, 1824, arts. 4-5, 7 Stat. 232; 2 Kappler 210 (1904).
quapaw-removal.quote: The Quapaw Tribe of Indians will hereafter be concentrated and confined to the district of country inhabited by the Caddo Indians, and form a part of said Tribe.
quapaw-removal.notes: Kappler page inferred from the URL slug. Art. 2 pays the four head chiefs $500 each "in consideration of the losses they will sustain by removing from their farms and improvements".
quapaw-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
quapaw-removal.sentence: The Quapaw are to be concentrated and confined to the district already inhabited by the Caddo.
quapaw-removal.source: Treaty with the Quapaw, Nov. 15, 1824, 7 Stat. 232

quapaw-removal.description: Treaty of May 13, 1833, art. 2: the United States agrees to convey 150 sections west of the Missouri line "in lieu of their location on Red River". Art. 3 has them removed at U.S. expense.
quapaw-removal.citation: Treaty with the Quapaw, May 13, 1833, arts. 2-3, 7 Stat. 424; 2 Kappler 395 (1904).
quapaw-removal.quote: agree to convey to the Quapaw Indians one hundred and fifty sections of land west of the State line of Missouri and between the lands of the Senecas and Shawnees
quapaw-removal.notes: Kappler page inferred from the URL slug.
quapaw-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
quapaw-removal.sentence: The United States agrees to convey 150 sections west of Missouri and to remove the Quapaw at its expense.
quapaw-removal.source: Treaty with the Quapaw, May 13, 1833, 7 Stat. 424

quapaw-removal.description: The 1833 treaty's own preamble records the outcome of the 1824-26 removal: the Quapaw went to the Red River, the tract flooded, crops were destroyed "year after year", and "nearly one-fourth of their people died".
quapaw-removal.citation: Treaty with the Quapaw, May 13, 1833, preamble, 7 Stat. 424; 2 Kappler 395 (1904).
quapaw-removal.quote: which was found subject to frequent inundations on account of the raft on Red River, and where their crops were destroyed by the water year after year, and which also proved to be a very sickly country and where in a short time, nearly one-fourth of their people died
quapaw-removal.numbers: about 700 Quapaw, per a population list in S. Doc. 512, vol. 4 (page not pinned)
quapaw-removal.deaths: "nearly one-fourth of their people" (treaty preamble, a government document signed by the U.S. commissioner)
quapaw-removal.dates: removal began 1825-26; flight back to Arkansas by about 1830-32
quapaw-removal.notes: This is a negotiated document, so the death figure is a recital agreed by the U.S. commissioner (John F. Schermerhorn), not a count. Strong as a government admission of the cost of the 1824 removal.
quapaw-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
quapaw-removal.sentence: This treaty records the Quapaw loss of nearly one fourth of their people at Red River.
quapaw-removal.source: Treaty with the Quapaw, May 13, 1833, 7 Stat. 424

quapaw-removal.description: Richard M. Hannum (Quapaw Agency, New Gascony, Ark. Terr.) to President Jackson, May 13, 1833, on the day the supplementary treaty was signed: the Caddo refused to receive the Quapaw; "that they were reduced to a perfect state of starvation; that many of the tribe literally starved to death."
quapaw-removal.citation: Correspondence on the Subject of the Emigration of Indians, S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 4, at 233 (1835) (Letter of Richard M. Hannum to Pres. Jackson, May 13, 1833).
quapaw-removal.quote: that they were reduced to a perfect state of starvation; that many of the tribe literally starved to death.
quapaw-removal.deaths: "many of the tribe literally starved to death" (Quapaw account as relayed by Hannum)
quapaw-removal.notes: Page 233 from the printed "[512] 233" marker; the text file puts "23S" for 233. The writer is Hannum (signature on p. 234). Only the Quapaw's report of what happened, as relayed by a government agent.
quapaw-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
quapaw-removal.sentence: Agent Hannum reports that the Quapaw were reduced to starvation and many starved to death.
quapaw-removal.source: Correspondence on the Subject of the Emigration of Indians, S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 4 (1835)

quapaw-removal.description: Quapaw preamble, 1833: after the Red River failure "they saw no alternative but to perish if they continued there, or to return to their old residence on the Arkansas, they therefore chose the latter". The Quapaw left the assigned place because it was killing them.
quapaw-removal.citation: Treaty with the Quapaw, May 13, 1833, preamble, 7 Stat. 424; 2 Kappler 395 (1904).
quapaw-removal.quote: as they saw no alternative but to perish if they continued there, or to return to their old residence on the Arkansas, they therefore chose the latter
quapaw-removal.notes: Shows the consequence of the 1824 order to concentrate with the Caddo, not troops.
quapaw-removal.checked: matched by script against the fetched text (Nov. 27, 2026)
quapaw-removal.sentence: This treaty says the Quapaw choose to return to Arkansas rather than perish at Red River.
quapaw-removal.source: Treaty with the Quapaw, May 13, 1833, 7 Stat. 424

quapaw-removal.description: Hannum, May 1833: of the Quapaw in Arkansas "many of them have been deprived of their improvements by the white settlers"; and the Red River country "will afford a dense white population. The Indians of course would be pressed to move, and would eventually be driven off."
quapaw-removal.citation: Correspondence on the Subject of the Emigration of Indians, S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 4, at 233 (1835).
quapaw-removal.quote: The Indians of course would be pressed to move, and would eventually be driven off.
quapaw-removal.notes: Hannum's prediction, written by a government agent. The earlier sentence about settlers taking improvements is in the same letter but not quoted.

quapaw-removal.source: Correspondence on the Subject of the Emigration of Indians, S. Doc. No. 512, 23d Cong., 1st Sess., vol. 4 (1835)
